outcome: The implicit graph conjecture (every hereditary family of at most factorial speed admits an O(log n)-bit implicit representation) was refuted by Hamed Hatami and Pooya Hatami in a preprint posted 25 November 2021 (arXiv:2111.13198), published at FOCS 2022 and digested/cited widely since; a scaled-down version restricted to 'small' (slower-than-factorial) hereditary classes was also disproved before the frozen date, in Dawson, Hoffmann, Masařík, Ossona de Mendez, Pilipczuk, Siebertz (arXiv:2307.11225, posted 20 July 2023, journal version SIAM J. Computing 2024). Both events predate the 26 January 2024 snapshot. No case, variant or restated form of the stated conjecture has been resolved inside the window; the only in-window activity is progress on a different, still-open conjecture (the 'Small Implicit Graph Conjecture' of Bonnet et al.) that narrows a bound but does not touch the statement given here.

counterexample.object: A hereditary family of graphs of factorial speed of growth (constructed via a probabilistic/counting argument, not an explicit family) for which every implicit (adjacency-labeling) representation requires labels of length n^Ω(1), refuting the requirement of O(log n)-bit labels.
counterexample.verified_how: Non-constructive probabilistic counting argument; the existence of such a family is proved but no explicit member family is exhibited (later work calls the search for an explicit counterexample the 'Explicit Implicit Graph Conjecture', which remains open).

summary: The bullet as given in this snapshot ('the implicit graph conjecture on the existence of implicit representations for slowly-growing hereditary families of graphs') is Wikipedia's own generic paraphrase of what is, in the literature, the single Implicit Graph Conjecture (IGC) of Kannan-Naor-Rudich/Spinrad: every hereditary graph family of at most factorial speed of growth admits an O(log n)-bit adjacency-labeling scheme. This was refuted by Hamed Hatami and Pooya Hatami in arXiv:2111.13198 ('The Implicit Graph Conjecture is False'), posted 25 November 2021 and published at FOCS 2022 -- a widely cited, expert-digested result (confirmed via the paper itself, its IEEE/FOCS publication record, and its treatment in later surveys and follow-up papers such as arXiv:2405.09011 and the ITCS 2025 paper arXiv:2409.04821, both of which state flatly that the IGC 'was recently refuted'). This event, and the conjecture's refutation, predates the 26 January 2024 frozen revision by more than two years, so status is open_stale rather than any in-window code. I also checked whether a narrower, slower-growing restriction of the conjecture (matching the 'slowly-growing' wording more literally) might still have been open in January 2024 and settled afterward. It was not: Dawson, Hoffmann, Masařík, Ossona de Mendez, Pilipczuk and Siebertz had already disproved the analogous conjecture for 'small' hereditary classes (growth rate n!^{c^n}, much slower than factorial) in arXiv:2307.11225, posted 20 July 2023 (journal version in SIAM J. Computing, 2024) -- again before the window. The only genuinely in-window development I found is arXiv:2409.04821 ('Adjacency Labeling Schemes for Small Classes' by Bonnet et al., posted 7 September 2024, published ITCS 2025), which improves the best known upper bound for small hereditary classes from polynomial (n^{1-epsilon}) to O(log^3 n) bits, and proves that small weakly sparse classes do admit full implicit representations. But this bears on a *different* conjecture -- the 'Small Implicit Graph Conjecture', a new conjecture introduced precisely because the original (and its small-class analogue) were already known false -- not on the statement given in this record. Under the scope rule (3.1), a bound moving on a distinct, subsequently-posed conjecture is a related problem, not a case of this one, so it does not change the status. No AI system appears anywhere in this line of work: none of the papers checked (Hatami-Hatami 2021/2022, Dawson et al. 2023/2024, Bonnet et al. 2024/2025) mention machine learning, LLMs, or automated theorem provers in their methods, and general searches for AI involvement in this specific conjecture turned up nothing relevant.
competing_reading: If 'slowly-growing hereditary families' in the Wikipedia bullet is read as pointing specifically at the small-class variant (rather than as generic wording for the standard factorial-speed IGC), the decisive event would instead be Dawson et al.'s arXiv:2307.11225 (posted 20 July 2023, journal version 2024) -- still open_stale, just with a different date and different credited authors (Dawson, Hoffmann, Masařík, Ossona de Mendez, Pilipczuk, Siebertz instead of the Hatamis). Either reading keeps the status at open_stale and keeps all in-window activity (arXiv:2409.04821) as progress on a different, later-introduced conjecture rather than a case of the stated one, so the classification is robust to this ambiguity; I selected the standard/factorial-speed IGC as the primary reading because it is the one with its own dedicated Wikipedia article and the one virtually all secondary sources call 'the implicit graph conjecture' without qualification.
what_would_settle_it: The Wikipedia editors' intended referent for 'slowly-growing hereditary families' -- i.e., whether the bullet was written with the classical factorial-speed IGC in mind (in which case it is simply stale, refuted in 2021/2022) or with a specific slower-growth restriction in mind (in which case it is stale via the 2023 result instead). Either way, resolving the small implicit graph conjecture (open, and the subject of live 2024-2025 research) would be the next event actually worth tracking under this bullet going forward.
